correctness.rationale: Theorem 5.1 and Remark 5.2 give S_{4p}−C_{4p} integral: only divisors 4 and 4p contribute cotangent blocks, C₄=−2, and the multiplier count for full divisor 4p is one. Splitting the alternating sum by parity gives C_{4p}=2P_{4p}(2p)−P_{4p}(4p). Independently, E_q(t)=((1+it)^q−(1−it)^q)/(2iqt) by its cotangent roots and its constant term, giving the stated e_j. For q=2p or 4p those even-index coefficients have denominators dividing p by e_j=(−1)^{j/2}binom(q−1,j)/(j+1) and the original denominator q; only degrees p−1 and (for 4p) 3p−1 can be exceptional. Factor E=B(1+R/B), where B is p-integral with constant term one and R is the sum of exceptional terms. In degree 4p the coefficients of log B have valuation at least −1: powers of B−1 have p-integral coefficients and the log divisor k is ≤4p<p². Multiplication by −4p makes this part integral. The log(1+R/B) terms of orders 1–3 give valuation at least −2 after −4p; no order ≥5 is possible, and in order four all factors must have degree p−1 in R. The fourth-order sign and −4p give p^3P_{4p}(q) ≡ u_q^4[t^4]B^{−4}=10/9−4/5=14/45 mod p, with u_q≡(−1)^{(p−1)/2}. Thus the same nonzero residue survives in C_{4p} for every prime p≥11, with no other denominator prime by Newton identities. For p=7 an independent exact log-coefficient extraction by integer partitions gives P₂₈(14)=90379872762811458892/49 and P₂₈(28)=34695770991787218624432158970/49; their prescribed combination is the stated C₂₈, with numerator 2 mod 7.
residual_risks: The finite p=7 extraction proves only that case. The symbolic valuation argument is needed for the universal law and does not classify composite odd parts or higher dyadic layers.
